query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an FCC matrix, a high density of additive-manufacturing–induced defects (especially grain boundary networks) couples with selective titanium oxidation to govern degradation during high-temperature exposure. Under oxidizing atmospheres, these defects accelerate oxygen ingress that promotes the preferential formation of a continuous yet mismatched TiO2‐rich oxide layer (competing with Cr-rich and Al‐rich oxides), which introduces local strain and stress. In reducing atmospheres, the suppressed formation of a protective TiO2 layer leads instead to the development of discontinuous, porous suboxides, which further enhance oxygen diffusion along defects. Both scenarios eventually invoke rapid, localized volume changes that exceed the accommodation capacity of the substrate, causing catastrophic spallation and failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an FCC-dominant matrix displaying high defect/grain-boundary density typical of rapid solidification.
generation.intervention: Post-process a set of identical samples with a heat treatment aimed at reducing grain-boundary density (coarsening grains without altering phase composition) and test them side-by-side with the as-built high-defect samples.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., 850–1050 °C) under controlled oxidizing (e.g., pure O2 at fixed pressure) versus reducing gas environments (e.g., 5% H2 in inert gas) for extended exposure durations (e.g., 100 h).
generation.structural_mediator: The density and connectivity of grain boundaries and defects that serve as rapid diffusion pathways, coupled with the spatial distribution of Ti at or near these boundaries.
generation.mechanism: High defect density accelerates oxygen ingress along grain boundaries. Under oxidizing conditions, this promotes the formation of a TiO2-rich oxide scale that is structurally mismatched with concomitantly forming Cr- and Al-rich oxides, leading to internal stress and ultimately spallation. Under reducing atmospheres, the limited availability of oxidant prevents the formation of a coherent, protective TiO2 layer and instead favors porous or discontinuous oxide formation, which exacerbates local stress concentrations. In both cases, the interfacial strain and the mismatch in oxide volume expansion in the vicinity of defects trigger catastrophic mechanical failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples with the high grain-boundary density (as-built) will exhibit faster oxide kinetics, the development of a heterogeneous oxide scale with regions of TiO2 enrichment, and earlier onset of spallation and catastrophic failure. Heat-treated (coarser grain) samples will show slower oxidation kinetics, more uniform oxide layers, and delayed degradation, especially in reducing environments where the protective effect of TiO2 is compromised.
generation.baseline: As-built samples tested under standard oxidizing conditions with known parabolic oxidation kinetics (e.g., from literature such as PMC9026100 results) including observed protective oxide formation and limited lifetime below 1050 °C.
generation.boundary: The results apply for exposures at temperatures between approximately 850 and 1050 °C and for atmospheres where the oxygen partial pressure is either high (pure O2) or low (e.g., 5% H2 in inert gas). Changes outside these boundaries (e.g., at much lower or higher temperatures or different gas chemistries) may invoke different mechanisms.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis extends the microstructural oxidation findings from additive manufacturing in PMC9026100::web::004 and the deformation mechanism shifts under oxidizing versus water environments from PMC9969177::web::009 by incorporating the specific role of Ti in this HEA. Although the individual roles of grain-boundary density and Ti oxidation are supported, their coupled effects under reducing atmospheres in this specific composition remain uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples: one in the as-built condition (high defect density) and one heat-treated to coarsen grains (reduced defect network). Expose both sets separately to identical high-temperature conditions (e.g., 950 °C) in both a pure oxidizing (O2) atmosphere and a reducing gas mixture (5% H2 in inert gas) for 100 hours. Characterize the oxide scale composition, morphology, and spallation behavior by cross-sectional electron microscopy, XRD, and mass gain measurements.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and compositional mapping (e.g., via EDS, TEM)
Mass gain kinetics and parabolic rate constants
Residual grain-boundary density pre- and post-exposure (EBSD)
Onset and extent of oxide spallation and catastrophic failure via mechanical testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If (a) both as-built and heat-treated samples exhibit similar uniform, adherent oxide scales and comparable failure times under both oxidizing and reducing conditions, or (b) if Ti does not concentrate at grain boundaries and no mismatch-induced internal stresses are observed, then the hypothesized role of defect-enhanced selective Ti-oxidation in driving catastrophic failure will be falsified.
